books.section: Topic 4.10 The Second Great Awakening, Utopian Communities

stimulus.text: The photograph shows the Oneida Community in New York in the 1860s and 1870s: a large brick communal building with a tower, set on open grounds where small groups of people walk and gather. The Oneida Community was founded in 1848 by John Humphrey Noyes as a utopian community in which members shared property and labor and practiced complex marriage, the sharing of spouses within the community.
stimulus.source_note: Description records only what the photograph visibly shows; the facts about Oneida's founding, Noyes, shared property, and complex marriage come from Princeton Review, Chapter 8, and the standard account of the community. Photograph: Oneida Commune, c. 1865-1875, by Moulton and Dopp, public domain; image viewed before writing.

source: original; stimulus describes a public-domain photograph of the Oneida Community (c. 1865-1875)
stem: Oneida differed most sharply from Brook Farm in which of the following ways?

options.text: Oneida was founded in the South, while Brook Farm was founded in New England
options.misconception: North and South differed sharply, so two communities can look like a North-South pair.

options.text: Oneida welcomed enslaved people as members, while Brook Farm excluded them
options.misconception: Slavery divided the era, so any two groups can look like a pair split over slavery.

options.text: Oneida reorganized marriage and family life, while Brook Farm reorganized work and leisure
Oneida was a Catholic monastery, while Brook Farm was a Protestant church
options.misconception: Religious communities differ by faith, so the two can look like a Catholic-Protestant pair.

rationales.A: Both communities were northern: Oneida in New York, Brook Farm near Boston. Neither was founded in the South.
rationales.B: Neither community is known for this contrast. The sharp difference between them was not about enslaved membership.
rationales.C: Oneida's radical step was complex marriage, the sharing of spouses. Brook Farm's radical step was sharing labor equally and valuing leisure.
rationales.D: Neither was a monastery or a church. Both were utopian experiments, Oneida religious and Brook Farm transcendentalist, but neither fits these labels.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what each community changed: Brook Farm changed the working day, sharing labor and leisure equally.
2. Ask what Oneida changed: marriage itself, through complex marriage within the community.
3. Compare the two: one rebuilt work, the other rebuilt the family, and both called it a better life.
Background: Brook Farm was founded by the transcendentalist George Ripley near Boston in 1841.
Remember: to compare utopias, ask what each one dared to rebuild.

figures.caption: The Oneida Community in New York, photographed about 1865-1875. Members shared one large home.
figures.alt: An 1860s photograph of the Oneida Community's large brick communal building with a tower, set on open grounds with people walking
